Two families of products: baked and fried

Your five products fall into two groups. **Baked** products (bread, cake, meat pie) are cooked by hot, dry air in an oven. **Fried** products (chin chin, puff-puff) are cooked by hot oil in a pot or fryer. Fried snacks need only a gas or kerosene stove and a deep pot, so they are the cheapest way to start. Baked products need an oven, either a gas cooker oven, an electric oven or a locally made charcoal or gas baking oven, but they usually sell at a higher price per piece.

Why shelf life decides your selling plan

Shelf life is how long a product stays safe and pleasant to eat. A product with a **short shelf life**, like puff-puff or meat pie, must be made close to the time of sale. You cook in the morning and sell by afternoon, so you need a nearby, steady customer group: a school, an office, a market lane. A product with a **long shelf life**, like well-made chin chin, can be made once or twice a week, packed in sealed bags and sold slowly through shops and online orders. Many small producers combine both: chin chin as the steady earner, and puff-puff or meat pie as a daily fresh line.

A recipe is not magic. Every ingredient has a job. When you understand those jobs, you can follow a recipe better, fix problems, and stop wasting flour. This lesson explains the five things that control almost every baked or fried snack: **flour and gluten, raising agents, fat, sugar, and heat**.
A loaf of bread
A soft loaf is the result of gluten, yeast gas and oven heat working together.
Flour and gluten

Wheat flour contains two proteins, **glutenin and gliadin**. When you add water and mix, they join to form **gluten**, a stretchy network. Kneading makes that network stronger and more elastic, like a net of rubber bands. In bread, this net traps the gas made by yeast so the dough rises and the loaf is chewy and light. In pastry and cake, you want the opposite: a short, tender bite, so you mix gently and briefly.

Flour with **more protein** forms stronger gluten. Bread flour is a higher-protein flour; cake and pastry flours are lower. Most Nigerian home bakers use one all-purpose wheat flour for everything and adjust the method: long kneading for bread, light rubbing and little water for pastry. Check the protein figure on your flour bag's nutrition panel if it is printed, and note it in your records.

Fat, sugar, eggs and salt

**Fat** (margarine, butter, oil) coats flour proteins and shortens gluten strands. That is why pastry with plenty of cold fat is crumbly and flaky. Fat also adds flavour and keeps bread and cake soft for longer.
**Sugar** sweetens, feeds yeast, helps crusts brown, and holds moisture so cakes stay soft. Too much sugar in fried dough makes it brown too fast on the outside before the inside cooks.
**Eggs** bind ingredients together, add richness, trap air when beaten, and set firm when heated, giving cake its structure.
**Salt** adds flavour and controls yeast so bread does not over-rise. Bread without salt tastes flat.
Heat: oven and oil temperatures

Heat sets the structure, cooks the starch and browns the surface. Too low and products are pale, greasy or doughy. Too high and they burn outside while staying raw inside. Use an **oven thermometer** if you can, because many home and local ovens run hotter or cooler than their dial says. For frying, a **deep-fry thermometer** removes guesswork. Without one, drop in a small piece of dough: it should sink slightly, then rise and bubble steadily within a few seconds.

When you sell food, your customers trust you with their health. A single batch of meat pie with spoiled filling can make many people ill and end your business. The World Health Organization (WHO) sums up safe food handling in **Five Keys to Safer Food**. They are simple, and they apply directly to your kitchen.
A person washing hands at a sink
Clean hands and surfaces are the first of the WHO Five Keys.
WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
Keep clean
Separate raw and cooked
Cook thoroughly
Keep food at safe temperatures
Use safe water and raw materials
These five habits prevent most foodborne illness in a small kitchen.
Key 1: Keep clean

Wash your hands with soap and clean water before handling food and often during work, especially after the toilet, after touching raw meat or eggs, after handling money and after touching your phone. Wash and sanitise surfaces and equipment. Keep insects, rodents and pets out of the work area. Tie back hair, cover it, remove rings and bracelets, and do not cook for sale when you have diarrhoea, vomiting or an infected cut.
Key 2: Separate raw and cooked

Raw minced meat for meat pie filling carries bacteria. Use a separate board and knife for raw meat, or wash them thoroughly with hot soapy water before using them for anything else. Never put cooked filling back into the bowl that held raw meat. Store raw meat below cooked or ready-to-eat food in the fridge so juices cannot drip onto it.
Key 3: Cook thoroughly

Cook minced meat until no pink remains and the juices run clear. WHO advises cooking food to at least **70 C** at the centre; a food thermometer lets you check. Cook the filling fully on the stove before it goes into the pastry, because the oven time for meat pie is mainly to cook the pastry, not the raw meat.
Key 4: Keep food at safe temperatures

Bacteria multiply fastest between **5 C and 60 C**, the temperature danger zone. Do not leave cooked filling or meat pies at room temperature for more than **2 hours**. If you cook filling the night before, cool it quickly in a shallow container and refrigerate it below 5 C. Thaw frozen meat in the fridge, not on the counter. Sell meat pies the same day, and do not keep unsold meat pies in a warm display case overnight.
Key 5: Use safe water and raw materials

Use treated or boiled water for dough and washing. Buy flour, margarine and eggs from sellers with good turnover, check dates and packaging, and reject flour with weevils, a musty smell or damp lumps. Do not use eggs with cracked shells. Frying oil that is dark, smoky, foamy or smells sharp has broken down and should be discarded.

Store dry ingredients off the floor, in sealed containers, away from damp walls and direct sun. Label each container with the date you opened it and use older stock first. Keep margarine and eggs cool. A tidy store protects your money as well as your customers.
Hot oil and gas

Never leave hot oil unattended and keep children away from the stove. Lower food into oil gently with a spoon, away from you. If oil catches fire, turn off the gas if you can reach it safely and cover the pot with a lid or fire blanket. Never pour water on an oil fire. Keep a fire extinguisher or fire blanket nearby, keep the gas cylinder upright and ventilated, and check hoses for leaks with soapy water, not a flame.

Professional bakers weigh their ingredients. A cup of flour can weigh anywhere from about 120 g to 160 g depending on how you scoop it, and that difference is enough to turn soft dough into hard dough. Never fill pastry with hot or raw filling
Hot filling melts the fat in the pastry and makes the base soggy. Raw meat may not reach a safe temperature in the oven. Always cook the filling fully, then cool it before filling.
**Keep it cold**: cold fat makes flaky layers. On hot days, chill the flour and work early in the morning.
**Do not overwork**: stop mixing as soon as the dough holds together, or gluten develops and the pastry turns hard.
**Roll evenly**: thin spots burn and leak; thick spots stay raw.
**Seal well**: press the edges firmly with a fork so the filling does not burst out.
**Bake fully**: lift one pie and check that the base is golden, not pale and soft.
Pound cake (one 20 cm round tin)

A classic pound cake uses **equal weights** of fat, sugar, eggs and flour, which makes it easy to remember: 250 g margarine or butter, 250 g sugar, 250 g eggs (about 5 medium eggs out of the shell), 250 g flour, plus 1 teaspoon baking powder, 1 teaspoon vanilla and a pinch of salt. Cream the soft fat and sugar for 5 to 8 minutes until pale and fluffy, beat in the eggs one at a time, then gently fold in the flour and baking powder. Bake in a greased and lined tin at about 170 C for 45 to 60 minutes, until a skewer in the centre comes out clean. Do not open the oven door in the first half of baking, or the cake may sink.

In this lesson you will bake one loaf, then use a tasting panel to improve it, the same loop you will use for every product you sell.

Mix flour, sugar, yeast and salt. Add lukewarm water and bring together into a rough dough.
Knead on a clean table for 10 to 15 minutes. Add the soft margarine after the first few minutes and knead until the dough is smooth and springy.
Do the **windowpane test**: stretch a small piece thin between your fingers. If it stretches thin enough to let light through without tearing, the gluten is ready.
Put the dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and leave in a warm place for about 1 hour, until doubled.
Press out the air, shape into a tight log, and place in a greased loaf tin, seam down.
Cover and let it rise again for 30 to 45 minutes, until it rises just above the rim of the tin.
Bake at about 200 C for 25 to 30 minutes until deep golden. Tip it out and tap the bottom: it should sound hollow. If you have a probe thermometer, the centre should reach about 90 C or more.
Cool on a rack for at least an hour before slicing, or the inside will be gummy.
Rising times are a guide

Yeast works faster in a hot kitchen and slower on harmattan mornings or in air conditioning. Judge the dough by size and feel, not only by the clock. A gentle finger press that springs back slowly means it is ready.

Many loaves sold in Nigeria are softer and sweeter than this basic one because they contain more sugar and fat. Once your basic loaf works, you can raise sugar towards 10 to 12% and fat towards 8 to 10% of the flour weight, one step at a time, and record how the softness and colour change. More sugar browns faster, so watch the crust.

Selling food is a promise. Your label tells the customer what is inside, how much there is, who made it and until when it is good. An honest label protects people with food allergies, builds trust with shops, and is required for packaged food sold in Nigeria. This lesson covers allergens, label contents, shelf life and the first steps towards NAFDAC registration.
A blank product label tag
A clear label tells customers what is inside, who made it, and when it should be eaten by.
Allergens in your products

An **allergen** is an ingredient that can cause a serious reaction in some people. Reactions range from a rash to difficulty breathing. You cannot see which customer is allergic, so you must declare allergens on the label and be ready to answer questions honestly.
Allergen
Where it appears in this course
Wheat (gluten)
All five products: flour is the main ingredient
Eggs
Chin chin, meat pie pastry egg wash, cake
Milk
Chin chin (milk), butter, some margarines and cake recipes
Soy
Some margarines and vegetable oils; check the label of what you buy
Groundnuts and tree nuts
Only if you add them, or use groundnut oil; also a risk if you share equipment with nut snacks
Do not claim what you cannot prove

Never write 'gluten-free', 'sugar-free', 'cures' or 'healthy for diabetics' on your snacks. These are claims you cannot support, and nutritional claims on packaged food must be backed by evidence. If you use the same oil to fry groundnuts, say so, because traces can transfer.
What goes on a pre-packaged food label
Nigeria's NAFDAC Pre-packaged Food (Labelling) Regulations 2022 set out what a label must show. The main elements are:
The **name of the food**, describing what it really is, for example 'Chin Chin (fried sweet wheat snack)'
**Ingredients in descending order of weight**, with allergens clearly indicated
**Net content** in metric units, grams for solids
**Date of manufacture and expiry date**, written in full with day, month and year
**Name and address** of the manufacturer
A **batch number** so each production run can be traced
All information in **English**, with no false or misleading words or pictures
Once registered, the product's **NAFDAC registration number**
Worked example: a chin chin label
For example, Uche in Enugu packs chin chin in 150 g pouches for two neighbourhood shops.
Name: Mama Uche's Chin Chin, fried sweet wheat snack.
Ingredients: wheat flour, sugar, margarine (vegetable oils, water, salt, milk solids), vegetable oil, egg, milk, nutmeg, baking powder, salt. Allergens: wheat (gluten), egg, milk; may contain soy.
Net weight: 150 g. Made: 03 October 2026. Expiry: 03 November 2026. Batch: CC-261003.
Made by: her registered business name and full address, plus a phone number for complaints.
The label lists everything a customer needs. Uche bases the expiry date on her own storage test, not on a guess, and records batch CC-261003 in her production book.
Setting shelf life honestly

Shelf life depends on moisture, fat, packaging and storage. Dry, well-sealed chin chin keeps much longer than bread or cake, but the fat in it slowly goes **rancid**, giving a stale, paint-like smell. Test your own: keep sealed packs from one batch at room temperature, open one each week, and note when the taste, smell or crunch changes. Set your expiry date safely before that point. Fresh products like meat pie and puff-puff should be sold and eaten the same day.

Packaging matters for shelf life and safety too. Use clean, food-grade pouches, jars or boxes, never reused cement, chemical or fertiliser bags. Heat-sealed pouches keep moisture out of chin chin far better than knotted nylon. Add a short storage line to the label, such as 'Store in a cool, dry place. Reseal after opening.' Keep packed stock off the floor and away from sunlight, which speeds up rancidity.

Pre-packaged food made in Nigeria for sale through shops and supermarkets must be registered with **NAFDAC** (National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control). The usual path is: register your business name with the **Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)**, prepare hygienic production premises, apply to NAFDAC, allow inspection of your premises and testing of product samples, then receive a registration number to print on your label. NAFDAC has a desk for **micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs)**. Fees, documents and timelines change, so check the current requirements directly with NAFDAC's website or your nearest state office before you spend money on printed labels.

Potassium bromate is a banned bread improver in Nigeria. If anyone sells you a 'bread improver', read its ingredients and refuse any product that contains it.

Many small food sellers work hard every day and still have no money at the end of the month. The usual reason is not laziness but **unknown costs**: gas, oil, packaging and broken pieces are forgotten, so the selling price is too low. In this lesson you will cost a batch properly and track a few numbers each week.

The batch record

A **batch record** is one page or one line in a notebook or spreadsheet for every batch. It should show: batch number, date, product, the weight of each ingredient, oil and oven temperatures, cooking time, yield (number of pieces or packs), rejects, and quality check result. You already used parts of this in Module 2. Now add the money.
Full cost of a batch
What your price must cover
Profit
Your labour
Gas, power, transport
Packaging and labels
Ingredients
Build the price from the bottom up; profit only starts after every cost is covered.
Worked example: costing one chin chin batch
For example, Uche costs one 500 g flour batch of chin chin. The prices below are example prices only (approximate, in naira); check your own market, because prices change often.

Ingredients: flour 500 g about 900; sugar 100 g about 250; margarine 100 g about 500; 1 egg about 250; milk about 300; nutmeg, baking powder and salt about 100; share of frying oil about 800. Total ingredients: about 3,100 naira.
Gas share for mixing and frying: about 400 naira.
Packaging: 10 pouches about 1,000 and 10 printed labels about 500. Total packaging: about 1,500 naira.
Full batch cost: 3,100 + 400 + 1,500 = about 5,000 naira.
Yield: about 700 g of chin chin, packed as ten 70 g pouches. Cost per pouch: 5,000 / 10 = about 500 naira.
She also wants to pay herself for 2 hours of work, about 1,000 naira per batch, or 100 naira per pouch. True cost per pouch: about 600 naira.

If Uche sells at 900 naira per pouch, she makes about 300 naira profit per pouch after paying herself. If she sold at 600 naira, she would only be paying herself, with nothing left to grow the business.
Setting the selling price

A simple method is **cost-plus**: true cost per piece plus a profit margin. Then check it against the market. If similar chin chin in your area sells at 800 to 1,000 naira for a similar size (example figures), and your true cost is 600, a price of 900 works. If the market price is below your cost, you must reduce costs (buy flour by the bag, buy packaging in bulk, cut waste), make a better product people will pay more for, or choose a different product.

Shops need their own profit, so they buy at a lower price than you sell to customers directly. Work out your wholesale price from your true cost first, so you never agree to a shop price that is below your cost.
Cutting costs without cutting quality
Buy flour, sugar and oil in larger quantities once you know your weekly usage, and store them properly so nothing spoils.
Buy packaging and labels in bulk; printing 500 labels usually costs far less per label than printing 20.
Reduce waste: weigh portions, fry in correct batches, and plan production to match orders.
Strain and reuse frying oil only while it is still clean and light; discard it once it darkens, smokes or foams.
Group baking so the oven is full each time it is heated, saving gas.
Four numbers to track every week
**Units sold** of each product
**Waste**: units unsold, burnt or rejected, as a share of units made
**Profit**: total sales minus total costs for the week
**Repeat customers**: how many people bought again

Write these four numbers in a simple weekly table, on paper or in a free spreadsheet app on your phone. After a month you will see which product makes the most profit, which day sells best, and where waste eats your money. Keep business money separate from household money, even if it is only a separate envelope or a separate account on Opay, Moniepoint or your bank app.

Review your costing sheet every month, or sooner when flour or oil prices jump. A price that was profitable three months ago may now be a loss. When you must raise prices, tell regular customers early and explain simply, for example that flour has gone up, rather than quietly shrinking the size.

Have a plan B

Payment scams

Fake transfer alerts and fake payment screenshots are common. Never release goods because of an SMS or screenshot alone. Open your own bank, Opay, Moniepoint or PalmPay app and confirm the money has arrived in your balance. Never share your PIN, password or one-time code with anyone, including people claiming to be from your bank.
Writing a good catalogue entry
**Name and size**: for example, 'Chin chin, 150 g sealed pouch'.
**Price**, marked with the date it was last updated.
**What makes it good**: for example, 'fried fresh every week, no preservatives added' (only if true).
**Allergens**: 'Contains wheat, egg and milk.'
**How to order**: minimum order, delivery areas, and how much notice you need.

Your photos must show the real product at its real size. If a customer receives a meat pie that is smaller than the one in your picture, you lose their trust. Photograph a product from your normal batch next to something familiar, such as a cup, so the size is clear.

If you give shops credit or sale-or-return terms, set a limit. For example, deliver no more than one week's stock on credit, record every delivery and payment, and collect before the next delivery. Unpaid credit is one of the fastest ways a small food business runs out of money.
Collecting payment

Most customers will pay by bank transfer or POS. A business account with a mobile money provider such as Opay, Moniepoint or PalmPay, or a business account at your bank, keeps business money separate and gives you a record of every sale. If you take online orders from customers you do not know, payment links from services such as Paystack let you collect payment before you start baking. For big event orders, ask for a deposit, for example 50%, before buying ingredients, and the balance before or on delivery.

Finally, ask happy customers for a short review or a photo you may share, with their permission. A real message from a school or a regular customer is more convincing than anything you can write about yourself.

Well-made chin chin lasts. You can make it once or twice a week, seal it in bags, and sell slowly through shops.

Baking science
Every ingredient has a job
Flour: kneading builds stretchy gluten
Yeast: alive, needs warmth and time
Baking powder: works when wet and heated
Fat: shortens gluten, keeps things soft
Sugar browns; eggs bind and set; salt
A recipe is not magic. Flour and water form gluten, a stretchy net. Kneading makes it strong, so bread traps gas and rises. For pastry and cake, mix gently, so the bite stays tender.
Yeast is a living fungus. It eats sugar and gives off gas, but it needs warmth and time. Very hot water kills it.
Baking powder releases gas when wet and again when heated. Baking soda only works with an acid, like yoghurt or lemon juice.
Fat coats the flour and shortens gluten. That is why pastry with plenty of cold fat is flaky.
Sugar sweetens, feeds yeast and browns the crust. Eggs bind and set firm. Salt adds flavour and controls yeast.

Yeast sachet opened two months ago
Water just off the boil
Fresh yeast, lukewarm water

Then the water. She used water just off the boil, because the morning was cold. That killed the yeast.
Next batch, she uses a fresh sachet and water that feels lukewarm on her wrist.
She covers the bowl in a warm spot. In about 45 minutes it has doubled and is full of bubbles, and the puff-puff comes out light and round.
Food safety
When you sell food, customers trust you with their health. Follow the World Health Organization's Five Keys.
Keep clean. Wash hands with soap before handling food, and after the toilet, raw meat, money or your phone. Separate raw and cooked. Use a separate board and knife for raw meat.
Cook thoroughly. Cook meat filling on the stove until no pink remains, at least 70 degrees Celsius at the centre.
Keep food out of the danger zone, between 5 and 60 degrees, and never more than 2 hours at room temperature. And use safe water, good flour and uncracked eggs.
Safety first
Keep children away. Lower food into oil gently with a spoon, away from you.
Turn off the gas if safe and cover the pot with a lid. Never pour water on an oil fire.
Keep it upright and ventilated. Check hoses for leaks with soapy water, not a flame.
Never leave hot oil unattended, and keep children away from the stove. Lower food into the oil gently, away from you.
If oil catches fire, turn off the gas if you can reach it safely, and cover the pot with a lid or fire blanket. Never pour water on an oil fire.
Keep the gas cylinder upright and ventilated, and check hoses for leaks with soapy water, never a flame.

Fixing faults
Three common faults and their fixes
Oil too cool or pot overcrowded. Heat oil properly and fry fewer pieces at a time.
Hot or runny filling, or oven too cool. Cool and thicken filling; bake hotter.
Door opened early, too much raising agent, underbaked. Keep the door shut; use a skewer.
A quality standard is a short description of what good looks, feels and tastes like, so you can check every batch. Most fried-snack faults come from oil that is too cool, or an overcrowded pot.
A soggy meat pie base usually means hot or runny filling. Cool and thicken the filling first.
A cake that sinks usually means the door was opened early, or it was underbaked. Keep the door shut and test with a skewer. Change only one cause per batch, and write it down.
Before it leaves
Before any batch leaves your kitchen, check five things. Even colour. Fully cooked inside. The same size and weight, because customers judge value by size. A taste test. And cooled before packing.

For example, Rukayat in Ilorin finds about one in five chin chin pieces pale inside. She fried bigger batches to save time, so the oil cooled. She sends only the good pieces and explains honestly to the shop.

An allergen can cause a serious reaction in some people, from a rash to difficulty breathing. You cannot see who is allergic, so declare them. Wheat is in all five products.
Eggs are in chin chin, the pastry egg wash and cake.
Milk is in chin chin, butter and many cakes.
Soy can be in some margarines and oils. Check what you buy.
And groundnuts, if you add them or share oil or equipment with nut snacks. Never write gluten-free, sugar-free or healthy for diabetics.

For example, Halima in Abuja must deliver 50 meat pies and 100 puff-puff at 10:30 am on Saturday. On Friday she shops, checks her gas level, and cooks the filling. She cools it and refrigerates it within 2 hours, and weighs dry ingredients into labelled bags.
